opus-5.5.text:
I think we're getting close, but I'd frame it carefully. An inflection point usually means a technology goes from interesting research to something people can't work without. For language models, that moment came when the models became good enough that ordinary users found real value every day. For world models, I think the inflection point will come from physical AI: robotics, autonomous vehicles, and other embodied systems.

The reason is data. Real-world data for physical AI is expensive, slow to collect, and often dangerous to gather, especially the rare cases, like a pedestrian suddenly running into the road or a robot dropping a fragile object. A world model that can simulate how the world evolves in response to actions lets you generate that experience, evaluate policies, and train systems at a scale the physical world can't support. Once world models are good enough that developers trust them for training and testing, adoption will move very quickly.

Where are we now? Over the past couple of years, video generation and world foundation models have improved dramatically in visual quality. But visual quality isn't the goal. The real bar is physical plausibility and controllability. Does the object fall the way it should? Does the robot arm's action actually cause the right consequence? Is the result consistent over long horizons? We've made real progress there, but we're not done. I'd call it the GPT-2 to GPT-3 phase: you can clearly see the potential, and early adopters are already getting value, but it's not yet universally reliable.

A few things will push us over the edge. First, scale: more diverse video and sensor data, and more compute for pre-training. Second, better post-training, so a general world model can be specialized for a particular robot, factory, or driving domain with relatively little data. Third, closing the loop: using world models not just to generate pretty videos, but inside the training and evaluation pipelines of real policies, and measuring whether that actually improves real-world performance. When that becomes routine, that's the inflection point.

I'm optimistic. I think within the next few years, world models will become a standard part of the physical AI stack, much like large language models became the foundation for so many applications. And open models matter a lot here. The field is broad and physical AI developers need to customize, so making strong world foundation models openly available can accelerate the whole ecosystem rather than just one company.

r001.rationale: The response discusses specializing general world models for particular domains and integrating them into physical AI workflows, but does not state that a newly released world model needs time to configure for robotics deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think we're actually quite close to an inflection point, and I'll explain why I see it that way.

If you look at the history of large language models, there was a long period where people were building language models, but the pieces didn't really come together until a few things happened at once: we had the Transformer architecture, we had enough compute, and we had internet-scale text data. Once those three aligned, you got GPT-3, then ChatGPT, and the whole field changed within a couple of years.

For world models, I think we're in a similar position right now. The architectures are mostly there. Diffusion models, autoregressive models, and the hybrids between them can already generate video that respects physics reasonably well, that maintains object permanence, that understands lighting and materials. The compute is there too. What has been missing is the data, and more importantly, the right kind of data. Video on the internet is abundant, but it's not organized around the question of "what happens next if an agent takes this action." That's the piece that physical AI really needs.

So the inflection point, in my view, comes when three things converge. First, when world models become good enough that the gap between simulation and reality is small enough for a robot trained in the model to work in the real world. Second, when the cost of generating synthetic experience drops below the cost of collecting real-world data, which is very expensive for robots. And third, when there's an open ecosystem, so that developers everywhere can build on top of these models the way they build on top of language models today, instead of every company having to train from scratch.

I think we're already seeing the first signs of this. Teams are using world models to generate training data for robots, for autonomous vehicles, and it's starting to actually help. It's not a toy anymore. My expectation is that within the next couple of years, we'll look back and say that this was the moment when world models went from a research curiosity to infrastructure for physical AI, in the same way that around 2022 was the moment for language models.

The one thing I'd caution is that it won't look exactly like the language model inflection. Physical AI involves hardware, it involves safety, it involves deployment in the real world, so the adoption curve will be slower in some ways. But the technical turning point, where the models become genuinely useful, I think that is very close.

r001.rationale: The response discusses world models becoming useful for robotics and notes that physical AI adoption may be slower, but it does not say a newly released world model needs time to configure for robotic deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by an inflection point. If we mean a model that can generate a convincing video, that is one milestone. But for a world model, I would look for something more: can it predict how the world changes when an agent takes an action? And can those predictions actually help the agent make better decisions?

For example, if a robot moves an object, the model needs to predict the consequences consistently. A video can look very realistic and still get those consequences wrong. So visual quality alone is not enough.

I think the inflection point comes when learning inside a world model reliably improves performance in the real world. That would let us use simulation to explore situations that are expensive or difficult to collect physically. There could be a very powerful feedback loop there.

I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t put a precise date on it. We need progress in action-conditioned prediction, consistency over longer horizons, and evaluation. The decisive demonstration will be an agent that becomes substantially more capable because it can learn from an imagined world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses world models predicting the effects of robot actions, but does not state that a newly released world model needs time to be configured for robotics deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what we mean by an inflection point. If we mean a model that can generate a convincing video, that’s one milestone. But if we mean a model that understands how the world changes and can use that understanding to plan actions, that’s a much higher bar.

For me, the important test is whether the model can predict what happens when you intervene. If a robot moves an object, can the model anticipate the consequences, compare different actions, and help the robot choose? And can it do that in situations it hasn’t seen before?

So I would look for the inflection point in usefulness: when learning and planning inside a world model reliably improves performance in the real world. My expectation is that we’ll see this first in constrained environments, then gradually in more open-ended settings. There may be a striking demonstration along the way, but the deeper change will come when these models become reliable enough to build on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses world-model milestones and usefulness in robotics, but does not state that a newly released model needs time to configure for deployment.
